topics.title: Temperature Scales & Thermometry
topics.notes:
Temperature is only a meaningful, measurable quantity because of the Zeroth Law of Thermodynamics: if two systems are each in thermal equilibrium with a third system, they're in equilibrium with each other. This sounds obvious, but it's actually what justifies using a thermometer at all — the thermometer is the 'third system,' and it lets us compare two objects' temperatures without ever touching them together.

Converting between scales is mostly arithmetic once you know the fixed points: Kelvin = Celsius + 273.15 (Kelvin has no negative values and starts at absolute zero), while Fahrenheit relates to Celsius by °F = (9/5)°C + 32. Past questions frequently give you an unfamiliar scale (Rankine, or a made-up 'X' scale with different fixed points) and expect you to set up a linear conversion using two known reference points — treat any unfamiliar scale as just a straight-line equation between two points you're given.

Resistance thermometers work because a conductor's electrical resistance changes predictably with temperature. The key relationship is T = 273.16 × (R_t/R_tp), where R_tp is the resistance measured at the triple point of water (a fixed, reproducible reference). This shows up constantly in past papers as 'given resistance at triple point, find the temperature for resistance X.'

KEY FORMULA: T(K) = 273.16 × (R_t / R_triple-point).

topics.title: Specific Heat & Calorimetry
topics.notes:
Specific heat capacity (c) tells you how much energy it takes to raise 1kg of a substance by 1°C or 1K. It's a property of the material, not the amount of it — this is the source of a common exam trap: giving two objects the same mass and the same heat input, then asking whether they reach the same final temperature. They don't, unless they happen to share the same specific heat capacity, because Q = mcΔT means a smaller c produces a larger ΔT for the same heat input.

Calorimetry problems (mixing two substances at different temperatures) all boil down to conservation of energy: heat lost by the hotter substance equals heat gained by the cooler one. When masses and specific heats are involved, this becomes a weighted-average calculation — for two water samples specifically (same c, so it cancels out), the final temperature is just the mass-weighted average of the two starting temperatures.

For an electrical or mechanical heating problem (an immersion heater, a resistor, friction), the heat energy supplied is Q = Pt (power × time) or Q = Fd (force × distance), and you set this equal to mcΔT to solve for whatever's unknown — usually c itself, or the temperature change.

KEY FORMULA: Q = mcΔT, and for mixing: m₁c₁(T_f−T₁) = m₂c₂(T₂−T_f).

topics.title: Thermal Expansion
topics.notes:
Most materials expand when heated because increased molecular motion pushes atoms slightly further apart on average. For a solid rod or beam, this is linear expansion: ΔL = L·α·ΔT, where α is the linear expansion coefficient — a small number, typically around 10⁻⁵ to 10⁻⁶ per °C, specific to each material. Past questions are almost always a direct plug-in once you correctly identify L (original length), α (given or looked up), and ΔT (the temperature change, not the absolute temperature).

Area and volume expansion follow the same idea but scale differently: for area, the effective coefficient is roughly 2α, and for volume, roughly 3α (since area and volume scale with length squared and cubed respectively). Watch for questions that give you a linear α but ask about volume or area change — you need to convert first.

Bulk modulus (K) measures a substance's resistance to uniform compression under pressure: ΔP = K·(ΔV/V), where ΔV/V is the fractional volume change. This is really the compression version of the same underlying idea — how much 'push' is needed to squeeze something by a given fraction. Liquids typically have very high bulk moduli (they're hard to compress), which is why questions involving water compression tend to produce very large pressure values.

KEY FORMULA: ΔL = L·α·ΔT (linear expansion).

topics.title: Heat Transfer — Conduction, Convection & Radiation
topics.notes:
The three modes of heat transfer differ in what they require to work. Conduction needs direct contact between particles — it's how heat moves through a solid, like a metal rod with one end in a fire. Convection needs a fluid (liquid or gas) that can physically move, carrying warmer, less dense fluid upward and cooler fluid down to replace it. Radiation is the odd one out — it's electromagnetic waves, and it's the only mode that works through a vacuum, which is exactly why sunlight can reach Earth through empty space.

Conduction rate follows H = kA(T_hot−T_cold)/L, where k is the material's thermal conductivity, A is cross-sectional area, and L is the thickness or length the heat travels through. This is essentially Ohm's law in disguise — temperature difference plays the role of voltage, and thermal resistance (L/kA) plays the role of electrical resistance.

Radiation follows the Stefan-Boltzmann law: the power radiated is P = eσAT⁴, where e is emissivity (how 'good' a radiator the surface is, from 0 to 1) and σ is the Stefan-Boltzmann constant. For net heat exchange between an object and its surroundings, you subtract the two fourth-power terms: P_net = eσA(T_hot⁴−T_surroundings⁴) — and because it's T⁴, small temperature differences near everyday temperatures produce modest radiated power, while very hot objects radiate dramatically more.

KEY FORMULA: P_net = eσA(T₁⁴ − T₂⁴).

topics.title: Kinetic Theory of Gases & Gas Laws
topics.notes:
Kinetic theory explains gas behavior — pressure, temperature, volume — as the statistical outcome of huge numbers of molecules in constant random motion. The core assumptions matter for concept questions: molecules are treated as point-like (negligible size compared to the space between them), moving randomly in all directions, and colliding perfectly elastically (no energy lost in collisions). Past papers frequently test which of these assumptions is being violated in a 'which postulate is NOT correct' question — the elastic-collision assumption is the one most often tested.

The specific (per-unit-mass) gas constant for any gas is R_specific = R_universal/M, where M is the molar mass in kg/mol. This is different from the universal gas constant (8.314 J/mol·K) — a common error is using the universal constant when a per-kilogram answer is expected, or vice versa.

Internal energy of an ideal gas depends only on temperature and the type of gas: monatomic gases store energy as (3/2)nRT (three translational degrees of freedom), while diatomic gases store (5/2)nRT (three translational plus two rotational degrees of freedom). This 3:5 ratio is worth memorizing directly, since 'compare monatomic to diatomic energy at the same temperature' questions appear repeatedly.

Reynolds number (a dimensionless ratio) tells you whether fluid flow is smooth (laminar, low Re) or chaotic (turbulent, high Re): Re = ρvD/η, where η is viscosity and D is a characteristic length like pipe diameter.

KEY FORMULA: R_specific = R_universal / molar mass.

topics.title: Thermodynamics & Heat Engines
topics.notes:
The first law of thermodynamics is just conservation of energy applied to heat and work: ΔU = Q − W, where Q is heat added to the system and W is work done BY the system. Sign conventions trip students up constantly — heat added is positive, work done by the gas (expansion) is positive and reduces internal energy accordingly. Always define your signs before plugging into the formula.

For an isothermal process (constant temperature, so ΔU = 0 for an ideal gas), all the heat added goes directly into work done: W = nRT·ln(V₂/V₁). This logarithmic form is worth recognizing on sight — any 'gas expands at constant temperature' question is asking for exactly this formula.

A Carnot engine is the theoretical 'best possible' heat engine, built from exactly four stages: isothermal expansion, adiabatic expansion, isothermal compression, adiabatic compression — no isobaric (constant pressure) stage is part of it, which is a favorite 'which is NOT a Carnot stage' trap. Its efficiency depends only on the hot and cold reservoir temperatures: η = 1 − (T_cold/T_hot), with temperatures in Kelvin.

The second law of thermodynamics is fundamentally statistical — it says spontaneous processes move toward higher entropy (disorder) because that's overwhelmingly the more probable direction, not because of some absolute forbidding rule. This framing ('statistical formulation') is itself a common exact-wording answer in past papers.

KEY FORMULA: ΔU = Q − W, and Carnot efficiency η = 1 − (T_cold/T_hot).

topics.title: Elasticity & Young's Modulus
topics.notes:
Elasticity describes how materials deform under force and (up to a point) return to their original shape once the force is removed. Stress is force per unit area (σ = F/A), and strain is the fractional deformation (ΔL/L for stretching). Young's modulus (Y) connects the two for stretching/compression along one direction: Y = stress/strain = (F/A)/(ΔL/L) — a large Y means a stiff material that barely deforms under load; a small Y means a stretchy one.

Different moduli describe different deformation modes, and past questions test knowing which is which: Young's modulus is for stretching/compressing along a line, Bulk modulus is for uniform volume compression (like being submerged in a fluid under pressure), and Shear modulus is for deformation where layers slide past each other (like pushing the top of a deck of cards sideways).

A useful physical connection: the speed of a transverse wave through a stressed wire relates directly to that stress and the material's density: v = √(stress/density). This is the same underlying idea as wave speed on a guitar string depending on tension — higher stress (tension) means faster wave propagation.

When a wire is stretched elastically, the work done isn't simply force × distance, because the force builds up gradually from zero as the wire stretches (unlike a constant force). Instead, work done = ½ × F_max × extension, the same 'area under a straight-line graph' idea used for spring potential energy.

KEY FORMULA: Y = (F/A) / (ΔL/L).
